claims.text: The target material is a Ta-based refractory BCC high-entropy alloy in a disordered solid-solution state.
Experimental melting measurements are infeasible and DFT thermodynamic integration is prohibitively expensive for the target alloy.
A Moment Tensor Potential can replace full DFT thermodynamic integration with a perturbation-based free-energy calculation.
The MTP should be trained on DFT data from elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary subsystems of the relevant refractory alloy space.
The training set must explicitly include high-temperature liquid and disordered BCC configurations.
An MTP can accurately represent local atomic environments in a disordered refractory BCC alloy.
An appropriately trained MTP can capture complex liquid structure and short-range order in the target Ta-based alloy.
Standard EAM potentials fail to model the liquid structure of multicomponent refractory alloys adequately.
Accurate representation of liquid and disordered-BCC local environments enables accurate solid–liquid free-energy differences without full phase-space integration.
The MTP formalism offers an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost.
MTPs learn a potential-energy representation from DFT energies and forces.
MTP-driven perturbation sampling avoids the exponential scaling attributed to full thermodynamic integration.
MTPs can accurately predict dislocation core energies as a function of local environment.
MTPs maintain sufficient accuracy for liquid structure factors in the target alloy.
The MTP-based scheme will predict free-energy differences and melting temperature within 5% of DFT benchmarks.
The MTP-based scheme will reduce free-energy calculation time by more than 90% relative to standard DFT thermodynamic integration.
Omitting high-temperature liquid configurations from training can cause extrapolation artifacts that produce physically incorrect free energies.
The scheme may fail when the target alloy composition lies outside the convex hull of the MTP training data.
